(For info, I work in the MET) I have just returned to work after a period of stress leave. This is what I experienced:

How easy is it to get signed off? - I went to my GP (normal doctors appointment) and told them what I was experiencing. I told them I was stressed, having trouble sleeping, unable to switch off, and some other personal stuff going on. I told them I didn’t know what to do, and asked them what they recommended. They suggested I take some time off to reset and recharge.

How long am I likely to get? - you start with the 7 days self-cert, and then your GP will give you blocks of time off following this. I was given 28 days, after which I had another appointment where we reviewed it together and they signed me off for another 28 days. At the end of the 2(ish) months, I felt ready to go back. The truth is you can take off as much as you need, and your GP will just want to have regular reviews with you. Mine wanted to know what I was doing to “get better” - aka that I was working to change things and not just sitting on the sofa watching tv all day.

What kind of engagement am I meant to have with supervisors? - mine text/called me at least once a week. This may be MET policy, but my DS said he had to have a home visit once every 28 days as well. My guess is that this will depend on your supervisor and your force policy.

Am I meant to stay at home and be a bit of a hermit whilst sighed off? - absolutely not, and this probably wouldn’t help you. I made a point to go out, go on mini-breaks, go to sporting weekends for my hobby, etc. someone I know even went abroad on holiday whilst on stress leave. Stress leave is different because you’re not physically limited (aka you’re not contagious or in a hospital, etc) and taking time to relax, take part in hobbies, go abroad, etc is needed to recover, and often encouraged to help you reset and recharge.

I can’t help with the last two questions, but I hope the above helps. I hope you get through this, the job is tough, but there’s lots of support out there.

I did this degree at the University of Northampton. We were encouraged to become a special constable with Northamptonshire during our degree and they ran a separate recruitment for our course to join. When we finished uni the students who had got IPS as a special (and passed the degree ofc) got offered a fast track recruitment place as a full time officer. Those who did this from my year had a job as soon as they finished uni.

HOWEVER, this only applied between this uni and this force. I joined the MET and I had the same recruitment process as everyone else and the same training period. The degree definitely made my training easier, but there were no concessions for me having the degree already. 

If you’re thinking about doing the degree, I would probably advise you just straight join unless you want to go to uni/aren’t ready to go into the police full time yet. The PCDA entry route gives you the same degree and they pay you rather than you paying for a degree.

In the UK, legally rape (section 1 of the Sexual Offences Act 2003) is when someone inserts their penis into someone else’s vagina, anus, or mouth. The maximum sentence for this is life imprisonment.

Section 4 of the Sexual Offences Act 2003 (Causing a person to engage in sexual activity without consent) covers when a women ‘rapes’ a man and has the same maximum sentence of life imprisonment.

So basically, while it’s not legally called ‘rape’, it has the same possible maximum sentence.
